DESALINATION: Cape Town marine outfall pipes foul desalination

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Since 2015 there has been a great deal of pressure on the City of Cape Town to address the issue of the marine outfall pipes. The Camps Bay Rate payers association and the Hout bay Ratepayers have constantly engaged the City about the problem which they continue to deny saying the sewerage largely comes from the storm water drains and Marine outfall pipes are an acceptable form of sewerage disposal used around the world. Prof Leslie Petrik, Prof Jo Barnes and Prof Lesley Green have become a thorn in the Cities side as they expose the state of the water by their peer reviewed scientific research. Now QFS Desalination plant has become the latest victim of this denial. They tendered to process sea water but found they were processing water closer to sewerage. The uncomfortable truth about the quality of the water in out but instead of dealing with the situation the City of Cape Town has chosen to litigate and renege on its contract with QFS

Summary:
Despite concerns expressed publicly and in scientific papers by Prof Barnes and Prof Petrik on the health risks of exposure to microbes, and more seriously, persistent organic pollutants such as contained in prescription drugs and household detergents (including natural and synthetic hormones) — the testing for which is not required by national legislation — the City maintains that the sewage pumped out through marine outfalls do not pose a risk to human health or the marine environment.
In 2015 the City commissioned their own report from CSIR and despite results in 2016 they released a revised version in 2017 but Petrik and Barnes and Green challenged its findings- but even the CSIR report said the Marine Outfall pipes must be having an impact
In late 2018 Petrik release a report on finding harmful levels of latest report pointed out the levels of chemicals in fish which City has dismissed and said you would need to consume about 147,000 kgs of snoek or 60,000 whole snoek at a single sitting in order to ingest the equivalent of one Dicloflam tablet as an example – high levels of ecoli in sand and toxic chemicals in the sea- report peer reviewed – missing the point of accumulated levels and impact of antibiotic resistance
The City of Cape Town tried to stop Petrik from publishing her findings by visiting her Dean and saying her paper not peer reviewed – which it was done later that year – they attack on the messenger rather than dealing with the issue. City issue scientific reports like from CSIR but they are not subjected to peer reviews



Further information:
The City has not made the results of water quality tests easily available to the public for the last five years. And the last results contained in their 2018 State of the Environment Report date back to 2016. Up until five years ago the City published an Inland and Coastal Water Quality report at sub-council meetings every six months, which contained the test results for the previous six-month period. So public access to city-wide results has been, for all practical purposes, non-existent since 2013, and for no clear reason.
The lack of information for 2017 and 2018 means there is no way for the public to know via the City’s mandatory testing, whether bacteria loads increased along the Atlantic seaboard during holiday season when visitors increase the amount of sewage, nor what the situation is in winter when rainfall is common and the predominant north-west winds are likely to blow the sewage plume shorewards. – the City also collects its samples. The City maintain that the storm waters are the problem but if this was so the whole City would stink of sewerage. The Cities Scientific Department sample the water and this is not done in a consistent fashion. Testing of the water done by the City and random places and intervals and that is what was the basis of the CSIR report which they acknowledge was inadequate
Sewerage is not treated although the City insist it is treated because it mushed through fine sieve
These were the test results which IX Engineers based the spec for the desalination tenders’ document. The outfall services Camps Bay and Bantry Bay, and was spewing out 2.4 million litres per day in 2016, according to a report by the CSIR. The Mouille Point outfall runs 1.7km out to sea. It pushed out 28.4 million litres of sewage in 2016- Salt River and City Bowl including hospitals. The Hout Bay outfall is 2.1km out to sea, but spews out 5.7 million litres per day closer to Dungeons, the world renowned big wave break.
Finally they have announced the upgrade to the Zandvliet works 10 years after fighting tender in court but all this overflow going into the sea
The Coastal Waters Discharge Permit, which came up for renewal in 2016.- City says they have applied- why not granted and one of the pipes goes into the Marine Protected area.
QFS are the latest victims- Petrik wrote to the City in 2017 saying reverse Osmosis was not sufficient- they went ahead. The City delayed commissioning desalination plants for a year during which time IX engineers the consulting firm of engineers had amle time to test the water, instead they used the Cities tests results. QFS found out within the first 2 weeks specs in the tender document were wrong, the water was closer to sewerage treatment. The tender required them to construct the plant within 2 months so they could not conduct their own independent tests. They alerted the City that water was not what they said it was-adapted plant at their own cost. Ready to deliver water before Day zero but the City delayed taking on the water but eventually took 180 million litres then stoppe.

The City after a meeting with the water board which Petrik attended became was concerned about the quality and so stalled the project. QFS were ready to supply the 2 Million litre a day in March but the City stalled taking any water until September.
In June 2018 the first rains came and cleared out all the storm waters and sewerage into Table Bay and the turbidity- the bits /sewerage in the water which averages about 20 shot up to 400. They were having to change the filters every 8 hours and they stank like pure sewerage.
QFS adapted the plant at their own cost- an additional 7.2 Million so they could keep producing the water despite the tender having been incorrect about the quality of the water.
The City have breeched the contract by not paying the fixed cost of R1.4 million every month- “ the rent” for the equipment. The contract was for R53 million which was to be paid off over 24 months. This contract was scrutinised by ABSA who were satisfied it was solid and they would get the money back and so granted the loan. The City have only paid R2,5 Million to date and they should have paid R21 million in fixed costs
First City refused mediation then would not release the report to QFS- despite them having paid for it.Then they sued for breech in High court after asking for arbitration now City trying for arbitration –could be fear disclosure because there are a number of reports they have done which havn’t revealed to the public. Now QFS is sitting in the middle of a massive upgrade in the Waterfront and holding up that development so now the City are desperately trying to evict them. City rather fight wasting tax payers money rather than honour a contract.

Script:


Link “Remember Day Zero there would have been scores of people here and those daily headlines with desperate pleas to save every drop of water, it’s hard to believe now with dam levels at 82% that just two years ago we were sitting at just 31% and the City of Cape Town was asking for help from everyone” Script: Local and international companies were offering desalination as a quick fix, but it’s extremely expensive, so after much deliberation, the City of Cape Town put out tenders for 7 desalination plants in November 2017.

Herman “We were quite surprised that nothing was done you know sooner because it takes quite a bit of time to get this planning right and get the right equipment installed. Script: Herman Smit, Director of Quality Filtration Systems QFS , says in the end only 3 desalination plants were commissioned, one at the Waterfront for 2 million litres a day to save the tourist hub, and two in False Bay delivering 14 million litres a day. But it was a mad scramble with only two weeks to tender, and just over 2 months to build. Herman “ I think it was a political move to make sure that that they were seen to do something about it to curb day zero. Although two million litres is not a drop in the ocean compared to what the city really needed.

Link:QFS are not newcomers the industry having been around for 23 years they are specialists in membrane technology which is the basis of the desalination process Script: Calling in its international partners, QFS delivered the plant by mid- March 2018, just weeks from day Zero. In retrospect, the building of the plant was the easy part, explains Musa Ndlovu Director of QFS Musa “We actually had to send our analysis to the lab. We informed the city that the quality of the water that is coming to our plant is quite different from what was in the tender document. It was more dirtier if I can put it that way.

Script: The raw water quality varied enormously – up to 400 times more contaminated than in the specifications. This meant there were more solids in the water which blocked the desalination membranes very quickly Herman “In normal circumstances you replace these filters once a month. But on the height of the problem last year we replace these filters every eight hours. We went through two containers of these filters within six months.

Script: QFS spent an additional R7 million complying with the drinking water standards in the contract, but the City would not take its water until May, QFS was putting clean desalinated water down the drain weeks before Day Zero Herman “The city asked us to do all these additional tests which were indicators for wastewater all these micro pollutants. Now these micro pollutants are all three pages long. Eventually it took us about six weeks to get most of those tested. We passed all the acute tests with flying colours the whole additional testing was uncontractual Musa”And we didn't understand why we had to actually do those tests because we built a desalination plant not a waste water plant.

Script: QFS say that the contract was structured that it would build the plant at its own expense, and be paid back the capital over 24 months, even if the City didn’t take the water as long as it was up to standard. Herman “They said no they're not going to pay us until we do all these additional tests which was uncontractual.

[11:37:50] you must remember it is quite a big move for a company like us to say listen we're going to help Cape Town to do this. The city is asking us to spend our own capital of 37 million and put it into the Waterfront. And then promise us to repay our capital over 24 months

Link: To date QFS have been paid just over 4 Million of the R53 million rand contract. Script: After mediation efforts failed, QFS cancelled the contract in May 2019 and took a lien over the property suing the City Herman “We are not going to vacate the premises until this whole issue has been handled and the lien will only be lifted if they do settle our claim. The City says the contract required it to pay for compliant water only, which it did. It says QFS wasn't able to deliver compliant water until May 2018, and then only half a million litres a day. From September, the City agreed to accept 2 million litres a day, but QFS only managed to deliver half that. The City says it dealt with the two False Bay desalination plants on the same basis, and hasn't encountered any disputes

Link: “For more than 3 weeks now we have been asking the City for an interview finally after taking legal advice they responded in writing Script: covering the impact of the marine outfall pipes to the QFS case... The basis of QFS claim is that the City didn’t reveal the true quality of the feed water, and so the tender design specifications were inadequate. If it had known, it would never have entered into the contract. The City maintains it never withheld information, QFS should have tested the intake water itself and build a robust plant to accommodate these seasonal fluctuations. But with two weeks to tender, QFS says it had to rely on the City’s tender data.

Musa “In engineering terms we can we could accommodate normal variations like up to 10 percent. But the quantity of water that is coming in was abnormal. Script: The City says it’s tests of the QFS intake water over the last year never revealed the levels of contamination QFS is reporting. It picked up DEET, commonly used in insect repellent, and Nicotine in the seawater, but noted QFS were removing it in the filtration process. VO: When the desalination tenders first came out, Prof Leslie Petrik from the University of the Western Cape, warned the City that reverse osmosis, the standard process to desalinate seawater, wouldn't remove these contaminants

Leslie: And if you look at the CSIR report which came out in 2016 they actually showed that the harbour was one of the most polluted places along our coastline. One does have to question why anybody would actually agree to put in a desalination plant when they know that there's a Marine outfall around the corner and harbour right next door.

Script: WE ASKED PROF PETRIK TO INTERPRET A SELECTION OF QFS RAW WATER SAMPLES Masa “And when you look at some of these findings what sticks out. leslie “I've seen the ammonia levels are high and the e-coli forms and the entocci ...show clearly that these sewage impact in that area where the intake is. …...so what QFS is finding afterwards, reflects what the city knew before. Script: The City denies Prof Petrik’s interpretation of the report, saying it doesn’t show that the water in the harbour is polluted and unsuitable for reverse osmosis. The debate of how polluted the sea water is around Cape Town first hit the headlines in 2015 when aerial photographs of the outfall plumes taken by Jean Tresfon went viral Clip 24 I am standing here at the Greenpoint sewage outlet which is one of 3 major marine outfall pipes in the City of Cape Town

Script: Currently they’re releasing half their capacity, but it’s still the equivalent of 11 Olympic swimming pools of waste water daily. The Greenpoint outlet flushes the entire City bowl right across to Sea Point. It horrifies local resident and dedicated surfer Dave Katz Dave: Everything that goes into the drain ends up in the ocean everything if it's not FAECES it's urine it's chemicals.If you took a panardo last night if you took a diclofenac for the pain in your leg it will be in the ocean in a couple of hours

Script: It was Professor Petrik’ research that set off alarm bells when she reported finding hosts of chemical compounds in fish in False Bay, including antibiotics, industrial chemicals and Anti-inflammatories, which will have a serious impact on the food chain over time
Leslie: Persistent chemical contaminants are worse than micro plastics. Because micro plastics might just get into your gut and might force it into the cells but the medicines are actually definitely going to pass into your cells and they're designed to be have a metabolic effect. Script: But the City maintains that currently these levels are so low, they have minimum toxic impact on humans. By expanding their Scientific Testing Services they committed to join the international research into their impact Script: This is Camps Bay’s outfall pump station. It disposes the waste water from Clifton to Camps Bay and despite the pipeline being 1,5 km out to sea, it’s just 750 metres off Maidens’ Cove. The pre-treatment removes sand, plastic, and other foreign material. The rest is pushed through a 3mm screen and released into the ocean. Disconcerted long distance swimmers collected their own samples, testing them at Swift laboratories Byron
[14:32:10]From our own test the results have shown that when the water looks clear, it's generally pretty good, when it looks dirty it generally is pretty bad.

Script: Byron Herbert, representative of the Camps Bay and Clifton Ratepayers’ Association has been pressuring the City to modernise the system since 2015. Byron[14:11:32]what we've discovered is that they'd rather find reasons as to why it's not a problem, than consider that outdated technology needs to start being updated and needs to be investigated as to what alternate solutions are.

Script: The City released an extensive report from the CSIR on the impact of the outfall pipes on the marine environment, which found the waste water is effectively dispersed by the ocean, but noted various areas of concern. The City continues to monitor the impacts and sent us this footage of the Greenpoint outfall, which was switched off at the time, to illustrate that there is no accumulation of sludge in the ocean. Script: Prof Kevin Winter is the lead researcher at UCT Future Water research institute masa [15:20 37 What is your response to the City saying that Marine Outfall pipes, this is something that's done all over the world. Kevin [15:20 44] Well it is done let's acknowledge that it is [15:21 15] But it's really what happens right before it enters that pipe that I think there really is the concern and there are concerns that raw sewage is finding its way into that outfall pipe. That's criminal to my mind. And there needs to be a greater investment in that treatment works.

Script: Responsibility for this waste water is the nub of the desalination dispute. The City say stormwaters and rivers flushing out the urban areas have far more impact than the outfall pipes. This air-conditioning fluid was quickly cleaned up, but the City responds to 300 blocked sewers daily. Contamination levels fluctuate vastly, especially after the rain. QFS says if the City had just taken responsibility for the problems with intake water, the situation could have been amicably resolved HERMAN: I think the rains that came in 2018 changed everything for the cities perspective. You know if it was still dry as we're sitting here we would have been heroes the City would probably have paid us double just to keep the Waterfront open for tourism Kevin [14:57:22] I certainly don’t like to see these cases heading for the court because that is not the outcome we are looking for and here is an opportunity for us to learn for a company that took the risk and innovated in what it was doing to be able to deal with the water quality that varies considerably in the Table Bay area Script And although the dams may be close to full now, Cape Town is rapidly expanding, and with it, the demand for water. Herman: And I think if in our view water the water crisis will surpass the energy crisis next year

ArtList Ian Post (Odyssey) Art0001 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 08 September 2019 - Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 25 October 2019 Script: Link “Remember Day Zero there would have been scores of people here and those daily headlines with desperate pleas to save every drop of water, it’s hard to believe now with dam levels at 82% that just two years ago we were sitting at just 31% and the City of Cape Town was asking for help from everyone” Script: Local and international companies were offering desalination as a quick fix, but it’s extremely expensive, so after much deliberation, the City of Cape Town put out tenders for 7 desalination plants in November 2017. Herman “We were quite surprised that nothing was done you know sooner because it takes quite a bit of time to get this planning right and get the right equipment installed. Script: Herman Smit, Director of Quality Filtration Systems QFS , says in the end only 3 desalination plants were commissioned, one at the Waterfront for 2 million litres a day to save the tourist hub, and two in False Bay delivering 14 million litres a day. But it was a mad scramble with only two weeks to tender, and just over 2 months to build. Herman “ I think it was a political move to make sure that that they were seen to do something about it to curb day zero. Although two million litres is not a drop in the ocean compared to what the city really needed. Link:QFS are not newcomers the industry having been around for 23 years they are specialists in membrane technology which is the basis of the desalination process Script: Calling in its international partners, QFS delivered the plant by mid- March 2018, just weeks from day Zero. In retrospect, the building of the plant was the easy part, explains Musa Ndlovu Director of QFS Musa “We actually had to send our analysis to the lab. We informed the city that the quality of the water that is coming to our plant is quite different from what was in the tender document. It was more dirtier if I can put it that way. Script: The raw water quality varied enormously – up to 400 times more contaminated than in the specifications. This meant there were more solids in the water which blocked the desalination membranes very quickly Herman “In normal circumstances you replace these filters once a month. But on the height of the problem last year we replace these filters every eight hours. We went through two containers of these filters within six months. Script: QFS spent an additional R7 million complying with the drinking water standards in the contract, but the City would not take its water until May, QFS was putting clean desalinated water down the drain weeks before Day Zero Herman “The city asked us to do all these additional tests which were indicators for wastewater all these micro pollutants. Now these micro pollutants are all three pages long. Eventually it took us about six weeks to get most of those tested. We passed all the acute tests with flying colours the whole additional testing was uncontractual Musa”And we didn't understand why we had to actually do those tests because we built a desalination plant not a waste water plant. Script: QFS say that the contract was structured that it would build the plant at its own expense, and be paid back the capital over 24 months, even if the City didn’t take the water as long as it was up to standard. Herman “They said no they're not going to pay us until we do all these additional tests which was uncontractual. [11:37:50] you must remember it is quite a big move for a company like us to say listen we're going to help Cape Town to do this. The city is asking us to spend our own capital of 37 million and put it into the Waterfront. And then promise us to repay our capital over 24 months Link: To date QFS have been paid just over 4 Million of the R53 million rand contract. Script: After mediation efforts failed, QFS cancelled the contract in May 2019 and took a lien over the property suing the City Herman “We are not going to vacate the premises until this whole issue has been handled and the lien will only be lifted if they do settle our claim. The City says the contract required it to pay for compliant water only, which it did. It says QFS wasn't able to deliver compliant water until May 2018, and then only half a million litres a day. From September, the City agreed to accept 2 million litres a day, but QFS only managed to deliver half that. The City says it dealt with the two False Bay desalination plants on the same basis, and hasn't encountered any disputes Link: “For more than 3 weeks now we have been asking the City for an interview finally after taking legal advice they responded in writing Script: covering the impact of the marine outfall pipes to the QFS case... The basis of QFS claim is that the City didn’t reveal the true quality of the feed water, and so the tender design specifications were inadequate. If it had known, it would never have entered into the contract. The City maintains it never withheld information, QFS should have tested the intake water itself and build a robust plant to accommodate these seasonal fluctuations. But with two weeks to tender, QFS says it had to rely on the City’s tender data. Musa “In engineering terms we can we could accommodate normal variations like up to 10 percent. But the quantity of water that is coming in was abnormal. Script: The City says it’s tests of the QFS intake water over the last year never revealed the levels of contamination QFS is reporting. It picked up DEET, commonly used in insect repellent, and Nicotine in the seawater, but noted QFS were removing it in the filtration process. VO: When the desalination tenders first came out, Prof Leslie Petrik from the University of the Western Cape, warned the City that reverse osmosis, the standard process to desalinate seawater, wouldn't remove these contaminants Leslie: And if you look at the CSIR report which came out in 2016 they actually showed that the harbour was one of the most polluted places along our coastline. One does have to question why anybody would actually agree to put in a desalination plant when they know that there's a Marine outfall around the corner and harbour right next door. Script: WE ASKED PROF PETRIK TO INTERPRET A SELECTION OF QFS RAW WATER SAMPLES Masa “And when you look at some of these findings what sticks out. leslie “I've seen the ammonia levels are high and the e-coli forms and the entocci ...show clearly that these sewage impact in that area where the intake is. …...so what QFS is finding afterwards, reflects what the city knew before. Script: The City denies Prof Petrik’s interpretation of the report, saying it doesn’t show that the water in the harbour is polluted and unsuitable for reverse osmosis. The debate of how polluted the sea water is around Cape Town first hit the headlines in 2015 when aerial photographs of the outfall plumes taken by Jean Tresfon went viral Clip 24 I am standing here at the Greenpoint sewage outlet which is one of 3 major marine outfall pipes in the City of Cape Town Script: Currently they’re releasing half their capacity, but it’s still the equivalent of 11 Olympic swimming pools of waste water daily. The Greenpoint outlet flushes the entire City bowl right across to Sea Point. It horrifies local resident and dedicated surfer Dave Katz Dave: Everything that goes into the drain ends up in the ocean everything if it's not FAECES it's urine it's chemicals.If you took a panardo last night if you took a diclofenac for the pain in your leg it will be in the ocean in a couple of hours Script: It was Professor Petrik’ research that set off alarm bells when she reported finding hosts of chemical compounds in fish in False Bay, including antibiotics, industrial chemicals and Anti-inflammatories, which will have a serious impact on the food chain over time Leslie: Persistent chemical contaminants are worse than micro plastics. Because micro plastics might just get into your gut and might force it into the cells but the medicines are actually definitely going to pass into your cells and they're designed to be have a metabolic effect. Script: But the City maintains that currently these levels are so low, they have minimum toxic impact on humans. By expanding their Scientific Testing Services they committed to join the international research into their impact Script: This is Camps Bay’s outfall pump station. It disposes the waste water from Clifton to Camps Bay and despite the pipeline being 1,5 km out to sea, it’s just 750 metres off Maidens’ Cove. The pre-treatment removes sand, plastic, and other foreign material. The rest is pushed through a 3mm screen and released into the ocean. Disconcerted long distance swimmers collected their own samples, testing them at Swift laboratories Byron [14:32:10]From our own test the results have shown that when the water looks clear, it's generally pretty good, when it looks dirty it generally is pretty bad. Script: Byron Herbert, representative of the Camps Bay and Clifton Ratepayers’ Association has been pressuring the City to modernise the system since 2015. Byron[14:11:32]what we've discovered is that they'd rather find reasons as to why it's not a problem, than consider that outdated technology needs to start being updated and needs to be investigated as to what alternate solutions are. Script: The City released an extensive report from the CSIR on the impact of the outfall pipes on the marine environment, which found the waste water is effectively dispersed by the ocean, but noted various areas of concern. The City continues to monitor the impacts and sent us this footage of the Greenpoint outfall, which was switched off at the time, to illustrate that there is no accumulation of sludge in the ocean. Script: Prof Kevin Winter is the lead researcher at UCT Future Water research institute masa [15:20 37 What is your response to the City saying that Marine Outfall pipes, this is something that's done all over the world. Kevin [15:20 44] Well it is done let's acknowledge that it is [15:21 15] But it's really what happens right before it enters that pipe that I think there really is the concern and there are concerns that raw sewage is finding its way into that outfall pipe. That's criminal to my mind. And there needs to be a greater investment in that treatment works. Script: Responsibility for this waste water is the nub of the desalination dispute. The City say stormwaters and rivers flushing out the urban areas have far more impact than the outfall pipes. This air-conditioning fluid was quickly cleaned up, but the City responds to 300 blocked sewers daily. Contamination levels fluctuate vastly, especially after the rain. QFS says if the City had just taken responsibility for the problems with intake water, the situation could have been amicably resolved HERMAN: I think the rains that came in 2018 changed everything for the cities perspective. You know if it was still dry as we're sitting here we would have been heroes the City would probably have paid us double just to keep the Waterfront open for tourism Kevin [14:57:22] I certainly don’t like to see these cases heading for the court because that is not the outcome we are looking for and here is an opportunity for us to learn for a company that took the risk and innovated in what it was doing to be able to deal with the water quality that varies considerably in the Table Bay area Script And although the dams may be close to full now, Cape Town is rapidly expanding, and with it, the demand for water. Herman: And I think if in our view water the water crisis will surpass the energy crisis next year

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Since 2015 there has been a great deal of pressure on the City of Cape Town to address the issue of the marine outfall pipes. The Camps Bay Rate payers association and the Hout bay Ratepayers have constantly engaged the City about the problem which they continue to deny saying the sewerage largely comes from the storm water drains and Marine outfall pipes are an acceptable form of sewerage disposal used around the world. Prof Leslie Petrik, Prof Jo Barnes and Prof Lesley Green have become a thorn in the Cities side as they expose the state of the water by their peer reviewed scientific research. Now QFS Desalination plant has become the latest victim of this denial. They tendered to process sea water but found they were processing water closer to sewerage. The uncomfortable truth about the quality of the water in out but instead of dealing with the situation the City of Cape Town has chosen to litigate and renege on its contract with QFS
metadata.Summary: Despite concerns expressed publicly and in scientific papers by Prof Barnes and Prof Petrik on the health risks of exposure to microbes, and more seriously, persistent organic pollutants such as contained in prescription drugs and household detergents (including natural and synthetic hormones) — the testing for which is not required by national legislation — the City maintains that the sewage pumped out through marine outfalls do not pose a risk to human health or the marine environment. In 2015 the City commissioned their own report from CSIR and despite results in 2016 they released a revised version in 2017 but Petrik and Barnes and Green challenged its findings- but even the CSIR report said the Marine Outfall pipes must be having an impact In late 2018 Petrik release a report on finding harmful levels of latest report pointed out the levels of chemicals in fish which City has dismissed and said you would need to consume about 147,000 kgs of snoek or 60,000 whole snoek at a single sitting in order to ingest the equivalent of one Dicloflam tablet as an example – high levels of ecoli in sand and toxic chemicals in the sea- report peer reviewed – missing the point of accumulated levels and impact of antibiotic resistance The City of Cape Town tried to stop Petrik from publishing her findings by visiting her Dean and saying her paper not peer reviewed – which it was done later that year – they attack on the messenger rather than dealing with the issue. City issue scientific reports like from CSIR but they are not subjected to peer reviews
metadata.Further information: The City has not made the results of water quality tests easily available to the public for the last five years. And the last results contained in their 2018 State of the Environment Report date back to 2016. Up until five years ago the City published an Inland and Coastal Water Quality report at sub-council meetings every six months, which contained the test results for the previous six-month period. So public access to city-wide results has been, for all practical purposes, non-existent since 2013, and for no clear reason. The lack of information for 2017 and 2018 means there is no way for the public to know via the City’s mandatory testing, whether bacteria loads increased along the Atlantic seaboard during holiday season when visitors increase the amount of sewage, nor what the situation is in winter when rainfall is common and the predominant north-west winds are likely to blow the sewage plume shorewards. – the City also collects its samples. The City maintain that the storm waters are the problem but if this was so the whole City would stink of sewerage. The Cities Scientific Department sample the water and this is not done in a consistent fashion. Testing of the water done by the City and random places and intervals and that is what was the basis of the CSIR report which they acknowledge was inadequate Sewerage is not treated although the City insist it is treated because it mushed through fine sieve These were the test results which IX Engineers based the spec for the desalination tenders’ document. The outfall services Camps Bay and Bantry Bay, and was spewing out 2.4 million litres per day in 2016, according to a report by the CSIR. The Mouille Point outfall runs 1.7km out to sea. It pushed out 28.4 million litres of sewage in 2016- Salt River and City Bowl including hospitals. The Hout Bay outfall is 2.1km out to sea, but spews out 5.7 million litres per day closer to Dungeons, the world renowned big wave break. Finally they have announced the upgrade to the Zandvliet works 10 years after fighting tender in court but all this overflow going into the sea The Coastal Waters Discharge Permit, which came up for renewal in 2016.- City says they have applied- why not granted and one of the pipes goes into the Marine Protected area. QFS are the latest victims- Petrik wrote to the City in 2017 saying reverse Osmosis was not sufficient- they went ahead. The City delayed commissioning desalination plants for a year during which time IX engineers the consulting firm of engineers had amle time to test the water, instead they used the Cities tests results. QFS found out within the first 2 weeks specs in the tender document were wrong, the water was closer to sewerage treatment. The tender required them to construct the plant within 2 months so they could not conduct their own independent tests. They alerted the City that water was not what they said it was-adapted plant at their own cost. Ready to deliver water before Day zero but the City delayed taking on the water but eventually took 180 million litres then stoppe. The City after a meeting with the water board which Petrik attended became was concerned about the quality and so stalled the project. QFS were ready to supply the 2 Million litre a day in March but the City stalled taking any water until September. In June 2018 the first rains came and cleared out all the storm waters and sewerage into Table Bay and the turbidity- the bits /sewerage in the water which averages about 20 shot up to 400. They were having to change the filters every 8 hours and they stank like pure sewerage. QFS adapted the plant at their own cost- an additional 7.2 Million so they could keep producing the water despite the tender having been incorrect about the quality of the water. The City have breeched the contract by not paying the fixed cost of R1.4 million every month- “ the rent” for the equipment. The contract was for R53 million which was to be paid off over 24 months. This contract was scrutinised by ABSA who were satisfied it was solid and they would get the money back and so granted the loan. The City have only paid R2,5 Million to date and they should have paid R21 million in fixed costs First City refused mediation then would not release the report to QFS- despite them having paid for it.Then they sued for breech in High court after asking for arbitration now City trying for arbitration –could be fear disclosure because there are a number of reports they have done which havn’t revealed to the public. Now QFS is sitting in the middle of a massive upgrade in the Waterfront and holding up that development so now the City are desperately trying to evict them. City rather fight wasting tax payers money rather than honour a contract.
